Children's names announce a broken relationship

Each child’s name carries a message people hear daily. The names grow harsher: a place of bloodshed, then no mercy. Verse 9 gives the third name and its reason. God says, “you are not my people.” That reverses his promise at the exodus (Exodus 6:7). Verse 10 begins with “Yet” and turns at once. It repeats the promise to Abraham of countless descendants (Genesis 22:17).
Threatened loss turns toward renewed belonging

The chapter says “therefore” three times (verses 6, 9, 14). The first two announce loss. The third surprises: God will court her again in the desert. Verses 19–20 list what he brings to the betrothal. He gives righteousness, justice, loving kindness, compassion, and faithfulness. These are the qualities the marriage lacked. Verse 23 then reverses the children’s names from chapter 1.
A household waiting period explains public loss

This chapter is five verses long. Hosea pays partly in silver and partly in grain (verse 2). He then sets a time of waiting with no intimacy (verse 3). Verse 4 applies that to the nation. Israel will lose king, sacrifice, sacred stone, and idols alike. Both its proper supports and its false ones are removed. Verse 5 says the waiting ends in return, so it is a pause.
Rejected knowledge reaches daily life and leadership

Verse 6 says the people perish for lack of knowledge. The lack is no accident. The priests have “rejected” knowledge and “forgotten” God’s law. Teaching was their work (Malachi 2:7). Verse 8 says they profit from the people’s sins. Verse 14 refuses to blame the women alone. The men lead in the wrong, so the daughters are not singled out.
Foreign help cannot heal the wound

Verse 12 says God himself is the moth and the rot. The nation’s sickness comes from him. In verse 13 Ephraim notices the illness and chooses a doctor. It goes to Assyria and sends to King Jareb. Second Kings 15:19 and 17:3 record such payments. Assyria cannot cure what God is causing. Verse 15 says God will withdraw until they admit their guilt.
Quick promises meet a charge of disappearing love

The words of verses 1–3 sound like true repentance. God’s reply in verse 4 is weary. The people expect him to be as sure as rain. Their own love lasts as long as mist. Verse 6 names what he wants: steady loving kindness, not offerings. Jesus quotes this verse twice (Matthew 9:13; 12:7). Verses 8–9 show what the people are still doing.
Hidden heat and foolish flight explain failed rule

Two pictures explain the kingdom’s failure. Verses 4–7 show an oven: plots heat up overnight and burn by morning. Second Kings 15 records four kings murdered in a few years. Verse 11 shows a dove that flutters between two empires. It has no fixed direction. Verse 9 adds that foreigners drain Ephraim’s strength unnoticed. Inside there is heat, and outside there is aimless flight.
Made objects and chosen rulers cannot secure life

Verse 6 makes its case in a few words. A workman made the calf, so it is not God. The verse adds that it came “from Israel.” The idol is homemade. First Kings 12:28 tells how the calves were set up. Verse 4 says the same about the kings: made by the people, not by God. What people make for themselves cannot save its makers.
Celebration gives way to lost land and children

The setting is a harvest festival (verse 1). Hosea says the celebration will end. Verses 3–5 link land and worship. In a foreign land there will be no wine offering and no feast. Verse 7 then shows how the nation treats its prophets. It calls them fools and madmen. The verse gives the cause: the people’s great guilt and hostility.
Prosperity has cultivated the wrong harvest

This chapter speaks in farming terms throughout. Verse 1 says prosperity fed the building of altars. Verse 12 describes a different crop. The people must sow what is right and break new ground. Unplowed ground takes hard work to open. Then they must wait for God to send rain. Verse 13 says what they planted in its place: wickedness and lies.
Remembered care interrupts the threat of destruction

Verses 1–4 are a parent’s memories of a small child. Verse 8 asks four questions in a row. God seems to argue with himself. Admah and Zeboiim were destroyed with Sodom (Deuteronomy 29:23). Verse 9 gives his reason for holding back. He is God and not a man. In verse 10 the lion’s roar calls the children home.
Remembered Jacob challenges wealth without justice

Hosea holds up Jacob as a mirror for his descendants. Jacob began as a grasper (verse 3). He also wrestled, wept, and sought God’s favor (verse 4). Verse 6 says “Therefore” and applies it. The people must turn as he did. It names three duties: kindness, justice, and waiting. Verses 7–8 show the opposite: false scales and pride in wealth.
Forgotten care gives way to destructive power

Verse 4 states God’s claim: no savior exists besides him. Verse 5 recalls his care in a dry land. Verse 6 traces what went wrong in four steps. They were fed, they were satisfied, they grew proud, and they forgot. Deuteronomy 8:11–14 warned of that very sequence. Forgetting after such care is worse than never knowing. Verses 7–8 show the shepherd become a wild beast.
Returning words replace false sources of help

Verses 2–3 give the people a prayer to say. It gives up three false helps named through the book. They are Assyria, war horses, and gods made by hand. Verse 4 gives God’s answer: he will love them “freely.” Their words do not buy it. In 6:4 dew stood for Israel’s vanishing love. In verse 5 God himself is the dew that makes them grow.
